title: The 10 Best Cordless Impact Drivers
subtitle: Ranked from live Amazon data — the tool that drives long screws and lag bolts a drill can't.
intro: An impact driver is the tool you reach for when a drill starts to stall: it adds rotational hammer blows to power long screws, deck fasteners, and lag bolts with almost no arm strain, all through a quick-change 1/4-inch hex. DEWALT dominates this category on Amazon, so the list leans that way, but there are strong value picks too. One thing to watch, and the biggest gotcha here: many impact drivers sell as a bare tool (no battery), which is great if you already own a battery platform and a trap if you don't. Each pick below says which it is.

avoid.name: GEVEELIFE 450 N·m 1/2" Impact Wrench
avoid.flag: An impact wrench, not an impact driver
avoid.verdict: This isn't an impact driver at all — it's a 1/2-inch impact wrench for lug nuts and bolts, with "impact driver" jammed into the title to catch your search. Wrong tool for driving screws.
reasons: It's an impact wrench, not an impact driver. The business end is a 1/2-inch square drive for sockets (lug nuts, bolts) — not the 1/4-inch hex that holds screwdriver and drill bits. Your impact-driver bits won't fit it.
450 N·m (332 ft-lbs) is automotive torque, built for lug nuts and heavy bolts. Point that at a wood screw and you'll snap the screw or strip the head instantly.

The listing calls itself an "impact driver," an "impact wrench," and an "impact gun" on the same page to show up in every search. When a product can't decide what it is, it's fishing for the wrong buyer.
If you genuinely need to pull lug nuts or big bolts, an impact wrench is the right tool — but that's a different job from everything else on this list, which drives screws and fasteners.

buyers_guide.q: Impact driver vs drill — which do I need?
buyers_guide.a: A drill bores holes and drives small screws with steady torque and a keyed or keyless chuck. An impact driver adds rotational hammer blows to drive long screws, deck fasteners, and lag bolts without stalling or twisting your wrist, using a quick-change 1/4-inch hex. Most people eventually want both; if you only drive fasteners, an impact driver is the one.

This is the biggest trap in impact-driver listings. A 'bare tool' or 'tool only' unit ships with no battery or charger — a bargain if you already own that brand's batteries, and useless out of the box if you don't. A 'kit' includes a battery and charger. Every pick above says which it is.

buyers_guide.q: How much torque do I need?
buyers_guide.a: Impact drivers are rated in inch-pounds. Around 1,400 to 1,800 in-lbs handles nearly all home work: decking, framing screws, and lag bolts. Over 1,800 in-lbs is pro territory for heavy or repetitive driving. All the picks here clear the home-use bar.
Brushless motors run cooler, last longer, and squeeze more drives out of a charge. They cost more. For occasional projects a brushed unit is fine; if you'll use it weekly, pay up for brushless.

Only within the same brand and platform. A DEWALT 20V MAX battery fits DEWALT 20V tools, a RYOBI ONE+ battery fits RYOBI ONE+ tools, and so on. Buying an impact driver on the same platform as a drill you already own means one battery lineup for both — a real reason to stay in one brand.
